meta.title: How BSP buys: a reverse-engineered acquisition methodology
meta.author: Syed Rahman
meta.method: Deal records rebuild every disclosed BSP transaction (7 companies, the Smith + Howard exit and 21 of 23 add-ons identified by name) from primary press releases fetched 2026-10-06 (Business Wire via FinancialContent mirrors, PR Newswire, bpigroup.com, smith-howard.com, comelectrical.com, broadskypartners.com, Franchise Times, Accounting Today, frontlinems.com, BV and Audax/SFNet releases). They are cross-referenced to the repo's SEC Form D, Form ADV, BDC schedule-of-investments and UK Companies House evidence in BSP firm profile, Thomas Scientific filings, Frontline filings, BPI filings, Punctual Pros filings, CET filings and Fair Harbor filings (retrieved 2026-09-24). quoted rationale strings are copied verbatim from the cited release; size signals marked 'est.' are the repo's labelled estimates, not disclosures. Patterns were inferred by tabulating seller type, advisers, lenders, SPVs, CEO outcomes and add-on timing across the deal records. Criteria weights are analyst inference from those patterns. cadence stats are computed in Python from the deal dates.
caveats: Weights, strengths and size bands are inferences from public evidence, not BSP's internal screening criteria.

BSP states 23 add-ons; 21 are identified by name here. One Punctual Pros add-on (the BSP portfolio page lists 2) and one Smith + Howard acquisition (the exit release says nine) could not be identified.
Fund I is $335.0M sold per the Apr-2025 Form D/A. The '$137M Fund I' figure in some repo files matches the BSP-FL LP deal vehicle (Frontline), not the main fund.
Smith + Howard is included only as transaction history (portfolio company, add-ons, exit) to read methodology; it is exited and has no opportunity build.

seller type adds 'partner-owned' to the requested enum for CPA and agency partnerships (S+H, BOLDT, Market Street, Smith Kesler, Horton Lee & Burnett, BPS); seller type is null where ownership was not disclosed (CET portfolio company, NCI, Arrowhead).
Lenders for CET, Smith + Howard, Fair Harbor and most add-ons are not public. Linking Thomas's DDTL to NCI and Horton's funding to debt or rollover is inference from timing.

Thomas Scientific close appears to be 2021-12-14 (Form D first sale, loan maturity); the announcement date 2022-01-27 is used for cadence. CET uses Feb 2025 (Form D first sale 2025-02-05) although it was announced 2025-03-19.
The Harvey & Company add-on program for Thomas dates to the Carlyle era (article dated 2018-05-12); whether BSP retained Harvey after 2022 is not public.
People are named only in their public professional roles as stated in press releases, SEC filings or firm websites. No personal contact details are included.
Earn-outs: none reported in any BSP-era release (the only earn-out in the record is Carlyle-era Denville, $3M).
methodology_narrative: BSP buys theme-first: each deal release frames the company as the output of a sector thesis studied in advance, from RJ David's 'over a year' in electrical services before CET to Adam Glucksman's watch on accounting before Smith + Howard.

Since 2024 the filter has narrowed to essential services. Punctual Pros, Frontline and CET are all non-discretionary, and Fair Harbor remains the only discretionary consumer bet and the only portfolio company besides Frontline with no add-ons.

Anchor acquisitions come from two kinds of seller: sponsor secondaries for the larger checks (Thomas from Carlyle, BPI from Svoboda, Frontline from BV) and founder or partner owners taking first institutional capital for the smaller ones (Fair Harbor, Smith + Howard, Punctual Pros, CET).

In secondaries the outgoing sponsor often rolls a minority (Svoboda at BPI, BV at Frontline), and the inherited CEO is replaced at about 13-15 months (Simmons to Haas at Thomas, Naidoo to Britt at Frontline) while founder CEOs such as Sean Taylor, Matt Buckwalter and John Duquette Jr. stay.

Anchor acquisitions are bought in banked processes (6 of 7 had a named sell-side adviser, and Punctual Pros went to 'eight finalists'). Berenson advised BSP on Thomas, BPI, Frontline and CET, Harris Williams on Punctual Pros and Frontline, and Morrison Cohen or Greenberg Traurig was counsel on every deal.
The first add-on typically closes 6-9 months after the anchor acquisition (NCI at 6.1 months, BOLDT 7.6, Horvath 8.0, NuWave 8.0, Market Street 9.0), and the median is 8.0 months.

Add-ons are small founder-, family- or partner-owned firms (Day Associates with 10 people, Smith Kesler with 30+, Horton with 120+). None of the 21 identified came from a PE seller, and many were sourced through relationships, such as Matt Buckwalter's decade-long tie to Horvath.

Add-ons alternate between filling in geography (Market Street, Smith Kesler, Horton Lee & Burnett, Horvath, Horton) and adding new capabilities that create cross-sell (VIP, Fahrenheit, Geels Norton, Message House, Agado, NuWave).

Each company is financed with a private-credit unitranche from a different direct lender (Apollo/MidCap at Thomas, PineBridge at BPI, PGIM at Punctual Pros, NXT and Audax at Frontline), with delayed-draw or amendment capacity sized for the add-on program.

Larger companies get a deal-named co-invest SPV (BSP-TS, BSP-BPI Holdings, BSP-FL, BSP-CET). Against a $335M Fund I, a company needing more than about $40M of equity depends on co-investors such as Carlyle AlpInvest.

Smith + Howard is the template so far: about 100 professionals grew to about 800 through 9 add-ons and a tech, AI and offshore build-out, and the firm was sold to TPG Growth after 3.7 years with William Blair and Baird running the process.

Thomas Scientific shows the value of leaving room in the debt for add-ons and a refinancing. For the next deals the implied rubric favors $3-20M EBITDA essential-services leaders in fragmented regional markets with a founder CEO who will stay and run M&A, a warm first add-on, and a credible tech-enablement story.

cadence_stats.basis: Portfolio company dates are announcement dates from primary releases, except CET, which uses the 2025-02-05 Form D first sale because CET says BSP became majority investor in February 2025 (announced 2025-03-19). Add-on dates are close/effective dates. Add-on rates use BSP's stated counts (23 total; S+H 9, PP 2) over years held to 2026-10-06 (S+H to the 2026-08-06 exit). Months = days/30.4375.

rubric_summary.scoring: Score each criterion 1-5 using its scoring bands, then compute sum(weight % x score)/5 for a 0-100 fit score. Suggested gates: >=70 is a priority portfolio company or add-on, 55-69 goes on the watch list, <55 is a pass.
rubric_summary.back_test_note: The weights are inferred from the observed deal record, not disclosed by BSP. Frontline, CET and S+H would score highest on essentiality and fragmentation; Fair Harbor scores lowest on essentiality, the criterion with the joint-highest weight.
rubric_summary.size_band_finding: The working assumption of $5-25M entry EBITDA is only partly supported. Estimated entry EBITDA ranges from ~$2-3M (Punctual Pros) and $3-6M (CET) to $14-20M (BPI, Frontline) and $40-55M (Thomas, COVID-inflated). The core band evidenced since 2023 is about $2-20M. Add-ons cluster at 10-150 employees or roughly $1-5M EBITDA, consistent with Frontline's stated tuck-in criteria (~$5M revenue / $1-2M EBITDA).

items.pattern: Thesis before target: every company release frames the deal as the output of a sector theme the team had studied in advance ('studied the electrical services sector' for over a year at CET; accounting 'we’ve been watching for a long time' at S+H; 'focused on the communications and advisory services space for some time' at BPI; 'thematic investment strategy within essential sectors' at Punctual Pros).
items.implication_for_next_deals: Bring BSP a written sector map (fragmentation, tailwind, 2-3 candidate anchor companies) before naming a company; a target pitched without a theme does not match how they buy.

items.pattern: The self-description narrowed from 'business services and consumer companies' (2022-23) to 'essential businesses' / 'essential services' (2024 onward). Every deal since Apr 2023 is a B2B or non-discretionary residential service. Fair Harbor (discretionary DTC apparel, 2022) is the outlier and has had no add-ons.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Screen out discretionary consumer products; residential services qualify only when demand is non-discretionary (repair, replace, code-driven).

items.pattern: Two seller archetypes, roughly half each. Sponsor-to-sponsor secondaries are the larger checks: Thomas from Carlyle, BPI from Svoboda, Frontline from BV. First-institutional-capital deals are the smaller ones: Fair Harbor (founders), Smith + Howard (first external investor), Punctual Pros (founder franchisee), CET (private owners). In 2 of 3 secondaries the prior sponsor rolled and stayed (Svoboda, BV).
items.implication_for_next_deals: For a larger company ($15M+ EBITDA), expect a sponsor seller and offer the outgoing sponsor a minority roll. For smaller companies, target founder or partner owners taking their first institutional capital.

items.pattern: Founder CEOs stay; CEOs inherited from a prior sponsor get replaced at about 13-15 months. Retained: Danehy (Fair Harbor), Taylor (S+H, through exit), Bleeker (BPI), Buckwalter (Punctual Pros), Duquette (CET). Replaced: Simmons became Haas at Thomas (Apr 2023, ~15 months); Naidoo became Britt at Frontline (Jan 2026, ~13.5 months). Each outgoing CEO moved to the board, and Simmons joined BSP's Executive Board.
items.implication_for_next_deals: For a secondary, underwrite a CEO-succession option (an operator from the Executive Board or the network) by month 12. For a founder deal, the founder's willingness to stay 3-5 years and run M&A is a gating item.

items.pattern: The first add-on closes 6-9 months after the anchor acquisition: Thomas NCI 6.1 months, BPI BOLDT 7.6, Punctual Pros Horvath 8.0, CET NuWave 8.0, S+H Market Street 9.0. Exceptions are Frontline (no add-on 22 months in, during a CEO change) and Fair Harbor (none).
items.implication_for_next_deals: Have a named, warm first add-on before signing a company. A target that can only be the company and never feeds one is less attractive.

items.pattern: Add-ons are small, founder-, family- or partner-owned firms, usually under 150 people and often 10-60 (Day Associates 10, Smith Kesler 30+, NCI 60, BOLDT 50+, Fahrenheit 140+, Horton 120+). None of the 21 identified add-ons came from a PE seller.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Build add-on pools from owner-operated firms that are succession-ready (founder age and tenure, family generation). Exclude sponsor-owned assets from tuck-in lists.

items.pattern: Add-ons alternate between geographic density and new capabilities. Geography: Market Street (TN), Smith Kesler (Carolinas), Horton Lee & Burnett (AL), BPS (SC), Quintana and Day (Northeast hub), Horvath (NJ). Capability: VIP (search), Fahrenheit (HCM), JMM (EBP audit), Geels Norton (cyber), Message House (research), Propper Daley (culture), Agado (sports), NuWave (energy-efficiency design/build), Horton (wastewater), Arrowhead (forensics end-market).
items.implication_for_next_deals: Tag every candidate in the add-on target lists as geo-fill or capability and pace them in turn. A capability deal usually supports cross-selling into the existing base.

items.pattern: Geographic expansion first fills the region next door, then makes one larger move. Punctual Pros went Central PA to Central NJ. CET went Worcester/Taunton to Norwell MA to Connecticut, and the CEO has ruled out NYC. S+H went Atlanta to TN, VA, Carolinas and AL before going national at exit. BPI went DC to Brussels and Berlin, then London, then LA and Miami.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Score add-ons on distance to the nearest existing node, with a bonus for one new adjacent state per year. Respect stated management boundaries (CET: no NYC).

items.pattern: Larger companies each get a deal-named SPV, and co-invest scales with check size. Thomas: BSP-TS LP $257.1M plus Co-Invest I/II $95.5M. BPI: BSP-BPI Holdings $90.0M. Frontline: BSP-FL LP $137.0M plus Co-Invest $30.0M. CET: BSP-CET Co-Invest $7.5M from a single LP. Fair Harbor raised at the issuer level ($30.7M), and no SPV was found for Punctual Pros or S+H.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Against a $335M Fund I, any company needing more than ~$40M of equity probably needs a co-invest SPV. Pre-sound co-invest LPs, including Carlyle AlpInvest (Frontline), when sizing the next company.

items.pattern: Debt comes from private-credit direct lenders, a different one on each company, structured as a unitranche with delayed-draw or amendment capacity for add-ons. Lenders: Apollo/MidCap at Thomas (a DDTL funded around the NCI add-on), PineBridge at BPI (facility amended the day the UK add-ons closed), PGIM at Punctual Pros ($1.4M undrawn DDTL), NXT and Audax at Frontline ($90M). No lender appears twice, and none was found for CET or S+H.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Size the add-on delayed-draw line at close and leave room in the debt for a refinancing, as Thomas Scientific's December 2027 maturity shows.

items.pattern: The same buy-side advisers recur. Berenson worked 4 companies (Thomas, BPI, Frontline, CET) and BOLDT. Harris Williams worked 2 (Punctual Pros, Frontline), Morrison Cohen 5 companies plus the S+H exit, and Greenberg Traurig Punctual Pros, CET and NuWave. Counsel splits by deal team: Morrison Cohen on business-services and consumer deals, Greenberg Traurig on residential and infrastructure.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Berenson and Harris Williams coverage bankers are the people most likely to see BSP's next company. Brief them on the theme map, and expect Berenson on any $100M+ EV deal.

items.pattern: Anchor companies are bought in sell-side processes: 6 of 7 had a named sell-side adviser (Jefferies/Baird, PwC CF, Koltin, Boxwood, Guggenheim, FMI), and Punctual Pros ran to 'eight finalists'. Add-ons are mostly relationship-led: Horvath (relationship of more than a decade), Geels Norton (years of partnership), Quintana ('Thomas approached us'), and a Carlyle-era program in which Harvey & Company initiated proprietary add-ons for Thomas.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Win anchor acquisitions through thematic preparation and banker relationships. Build add-on funnels through portfolio-company CEO relationships, outbound owner outreach and possibly a retained search firm.

items.pattern: The one exit follows a clear sequence: a regional founder-led firm, 9 add-ons over 3.7 years, investment in tech, AI and an India delivery center, then a sale to a larger growth-equity sponsor (TPG Growth) run by William Blair and Baird. Headcount went from ~100 to ~800 and revenue grew nearly 4x.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Plan exits around a 3.5-4.5 year hold and a sponsor buyer. A visible tech/AI and offshore-delivery story was part of TPG's quoted rationale. By hold length and add-on count, BPI (3.4 years, 6 add-ons) looks closest to exit-ready.

items.pattern: Connections run through Carlyle and MidOcean. The seller and management of Thomas knew BSP's partners from their Carlyle roles. Carlyle AlpInvest co-invested $12.5M directly in Frontline. Zachem, Glucksman, Kiser, Narain and RJ David are Carlyle alumni, and Jodi Kahn was a Carlyle operating advisor. Zachem (14 years) and Marlow came from MidOcean, whose theme-driven, operating-partner model and franchise-services focus BSP mirrors. Guggenheim sold Frontline to BSP and later advised TPG on buying S+H; Baird advised Carlyle on Thomas and co-advised the S+H sale.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Look first at assets held by Carlyle and MidOcean-adjacent sponsors and by BV- or Svoboda-style lower-middle-market sponsors. Treat Guggenheim and Baird as two-way counterparties (they sell to BSP and buy from BSP).

items.pattern: After the first deal, check sizes moved down market. Thomas used ~$236M of equity at close (with co-invest); its loan matures in December 2027. Later checks were smaller: Fair Harbor $30.7M, BPI $90M, Punctual Pros an estimated $8-15M, CET an estimated $25-45M. The exception is Frontline at $137M+$30M, a high-recurring-revenue asset.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Default entry is a $2-20M EBITDA portfolio company at a sub-$100M EV, built up by add-ons. Go large only with >85% recurring revenue (Frontline-type) and avoid peak-cycle earnings (Thomas's COVID-testing bump).

items.pattern: Operators are placed on boards at entry: Lynn Calpeter (BSP operating partner) chairs Thomas, Roberta Bowman (ESG operating partner) at Fair Harbor, outside director Kelly Romano (ex-UTC, ex-AE Industrial operating partner) at Punctual Pros, and retail veterans added to Fair Harbor's board. The Portfolio Resource Group, or PRG (Jodi Kahn, Sam Pawliger, Georgette Kiser, Aditya Narain) runs the growth plan.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Name the board chair and the PRG workstreams (tech/ops, finance, pricing, recruiting) in the first-round letter. Sellers cited BSP's 'dedicated operating resources' as a reason to choose it.

items.pattern: 'People-first' and culture language is used as a screening filter and as a closing tool, alongside seller equity rollover. BSP's own quotes cite 'people-first culture' at BPI and Punctual Pros. Founders roll into the company (365 Sherpas sellers become BPI shareholders; Svoboda and BV roll). S+H and add-on sellers repeatedly say culture fit decided the deal.
items.implication_for_next_deals: Offer founders of add-ons rollover into the portfolio company, not only cash, and test culture fit before price. In professional services, rollover is the retention mechanism.

items.test: Share of revenue tied to repair, replace, compliance, regulated or mission-critical outsourced work. Measure from service-line mix on the website, NAICS code and customer type, and for residential services the repair-vs-install mix and Google review volume.

items.criterion: Recurring or repeat revenue and contract visibility
items.test: Percent contracted or recurring revenue (Frontline 92-93% on 3-5 year contracts); membership/maintenance-plan penetration for home services; repeat audit/tax clients for CPA firms; consumables share for distribution. Sources: CEO interviews, FDD Item 19, service-agreement counts on the website.

Count of owner-operated firms in the sub-sector within 150 miles of the company (ZoomInfo/Census CBP establishments; add-on target lists). BSP pace is 1-2.4 add-ons per company-year, so the target is 10+ actionable candidates.

items.criterion: Founder or management transition readiness, with a CEO who will stay
items.test: Founder or family owner with long tenure who wants a partner rather than a full exit (rollover appetite). For a secondary, an identified CEO-succession bench. Signals: founder age and tenure, generation (Horton is third-generation), named second-tier leaders, a sell-side adviser engaged.

scoring_bands.5: Founder staying 3-5 years and leading M&A, plus a successor identified

items.test: Portfolio company: est. EBITDA $2-20M core (observed estimates from ~$2-3M at Punctual Pros to $16-20M at Frontline; Thomas at $40-55M was the outlier), equity check $8-90M with SPV co-invest above ~$40M. Add-on: $1-5M EBITDA or 10-150 employees (Frontline's stated tuck-in ~$5M revenue / $1-2M EBITDA). Estimate via PPP payroll, headcount x revenue-per-employee and Form D amounts.

items.criterion: Geographic adjacency, with a regional champion that can go national
items.test: Straight-line miles to the nearest portfolio company node (<=60 mi best). Regional share in the home market; one new adjacent state or metro per year. Respect management-stated boundaries (CET: New England only, no NYC).

scoring_bands.5: <=60 mi or fills a named gap

items.criterion: Thematic tailwind that BSP research has already identified
items.test: The target sits inside a theme BSP has publicly named (outsourcing and workforce virtualization; energy capacity and critical infrastructure; legal-IT outsourcing and cyber; housing-stock and weather-driven home services; transatlantic policy complexity). Evidence: a public BSP quote or strategy-page sector list plus a measurable driver (permits, deeds, regulation, rate cases).

scoring_bands.5: Named BSP theme plus a measurable driver

items.test: Gap between current tooling and best practice: field-service software, CRM, AI service desk, offshore delivery. S+H's exit cited AI and an India delivery center; Frontline launched the HELIX AI service desk; BPI has ChangeOS. Check job posts, vendor case studies and web stack.

scoring_bands.5: Clear 1+ turn multiple case from tech/offshore
scoring_bands.1: Already fully digitized or not applicable

items.test: Named leaders below the CEO, low key-person concentration, retention evidence (Glassdoor, tenure in releases), and whether culture fit appears in the seller's own language. BSP quotes cite 'people-first culture' at BPI and Punctual Pros.

items.criterion: Downside protection: earnings quality, cyclicality and leverage
items.test: Normalize for one-off peaks (Thomas COVID testing: federal revenue fell from $84-91M to $7-8M a year; BPI election-cycle billings). Leverage <=5x at entry with a DDTL for add-ons. Customer concentration <10%. Watch BDC marks after close.

items.implication: BSP's most-used buy-side bank, on every larger company except Punctual Pros and Fair Harbor. It is the most likely channel for BSP's next company.
Used on the residential-services and legal-IT deals; HW's consumer and business-services coverage sees lower-middle-market home-services processes.
Infrastructure/electrical coverage; first appearance came with RJ David's infrastructure theme.
Consumer coverage; used only on the 2022 consumer deal.
In CPA-firm M&A the specialist intermediary sourced both the company and later add-ons. Sector-specialist brokers are worth courting in each theme.

items.channel: Sell-side advisers BSP bought from (Jefferies/Baird, PwC CF, Boxwood, Guggenheim, FMI, Founders Advisors)

roles.role: PwC Corporate Finance for Fair Harbor
Guggenheim Securities exclusive sell-side for BV
Founders Advisors for Horton, Lee & Burnett

items.implication: Anchor companies come out of banked processes. FMI (electrical/construction) sold both CET and NuWave to BSP, so sector-specialist sell-side banks are repeat counterparties for add-ons.

items.channel: Exit advisers (William Blair, Baird) and buyer adviser (Guggenheim)

roles.role: William Blair lead and Baird co-financial advisor to S+H and BSP; Guggenheim to TPG

items.implication: Baird and Guggenheim appear on both sides of BSP deals (buy and sell). William Blair is the reference exit bank for professional services.

items.channel: Deal counsel: Morrison Cohen LLP and Greenberg Traurig

roles.role: Morrison Cohen, counsel to S+H and BSP

items.implication: Counsel is not a sourcing channel, but which firm is engaged shows which deal team is running the deal.

items.channel: Portfolio-company CEO and partner relationships (proprietary add-ons)

roles.role: CEO relationship of more than a decade
BPI 'really studied the German market'; sellers roll into BPI equity

items.implication: Add-ons mostly come from people the portfolio-company CEO already knows. Each portfolio-company CEO's relationship map is the first add-on list.

items.channel: Harvey & Company (retained add-on search; Carlyle-era Thomas program)

roles.role: Initiated four proprietary Thomas add-ons in six months for the sponsor at the time (Carlyle, 2017-2018)

items.implication: Part of the Thomas growth plan the BSP partners knew from Carlyle. A retained buy-side search mandate is a proven way to run a proprietary add-on program on a new company. Whether BSP-era Thomas deals used Harvey is not public.

items.channel: In-house thematic research by the deal team

roles.role: 'For over a year, our team has studied the electrical services sector'
'a rapidly evolving space we’ve been watching for a long time'
'focused on the communications and advisory services space for some time'

items.implication: Theme-first origination: BSP picks a sector, then meets the leaders. Presenting a theme map is the way into their pipeline.

items.channel: Capital channels: Capital Constellation/Wafra GP stake, Asante placement agent, co-invest LPs (Carlyle AlpInvest)

roles.role: Capital Constellation strategic investment announced with the first deal

items.implication: Co-invest capacity sets the maximum company size. Carlyle AlpInvest and the Constellation members are the natural co-investors for a larger next deal.
